hooks: Everyone's excited about autonomous supply chain agents. Gartner is also predicting that over 40% of those projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.
The agent didn't fail. The data foundation under it did.
Supply chain software with agentic AI is going from under $2 billion in spend to $53 billion in five years. Over 40% of the projects built on it won't survive that long.
drafts.caption:
Everyone's excited about autonomous supply chain agents. Gartner is also predicting that over 40% of those projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.

Read the reason list. Model capability isn't on it.

The causes Gartner names:
→ No governance structure - nobody owns the call when the agent's decision is wrong
→ No clean data foundation - the agent inherits the same broken master data your planners have fought for years
→ No success metric attached - the "pilot" never had a number that decided if it graduated

Meanwhile the market is real. Supply chain management software with agentic AI capability is projected to grow from under $2 billion in spend in 2025 to $53 billion by 2030, per Gartner. Organizations that get the foundation right are already reporting double-digit efficiency gains and decision latency cut from days to seconds.

Same technology, opposite outcome. The difference isn't the vendor demo - it's whether someone owns the exception queue on a Tuesday morning.

Before you approve the next agent pilot: who signs off when it's wrong, and what number decides if it's still live in twelve months?

hooks: 77% of pharma supply chain leaders now rank AI-driven demand sensing for new launches as a top priority. Most are still feeding it the same three inputs as 2019.
A launch forecast built only on sales history is already six months late on day one.
Pharma leaders aren't asking if AI can forecast demand anymore. They're asking if it can forecast a launch nobody has sold before.
drafts.caption:
77% of pharma supply chain leaders now rank AI-driven demand sensing for new launches as a top priority, according to the LogiPharma 2025 AI Report, a survey of 100 senior leaders across Europe and North America.

But a launch has no sales history. That's the actual problem a demand-sensing model has to solve.

The teams getting it right aren't just swapping the forecasting engine. They're changing the inputs:
→ Prescription and market-access data instead of only shipment history
→ A rolling SKU-channel-region forecast that updates weekly, not a static plan set once a quarter
→ Predictive risk alerts on the supply side - 53% of leaders are now using AI/ML here, up from roughly 30% two years earlier

The same report names the real blockers, and none of them is the model: internal resistance (70%), regulatory uncertainty, and a shortage of people who can read the model's output and act on it before the batch record closes.

If your last launch forecast was wrong, was it the algorithm - or the input nobody updated after month one?

hooks: Deloitte expects agentic AI adoption on the factory floor to roughly quadruple this year, from 6% to 24%. Only about one in five manufacturers say they're ready to scale it.
The sensor predicted the bearing failure twelve days out. The work order still sat in an inbox for nine of them.
Predicting the failure was the easy part. Nobody automated what happens after the alert.
drafts.caption:
Deloitte expects agentic AI adoption on the factory floor to roughly quadruple this year, from 6% to 24%. Only about one in five manufacturers say they're actually ready to scale it.

That gap isn't about the sensor. Most plants can already predict a bearing failure, a motor overheating, a line about to go down.

What's missing is what happens in the days between the alert and the fix:
→ Who owns the work order once the model flags it
→ Which spare part gets reserved automatically instead of requested by email
→ What triggers a line-speed change while the fix gets scheduled

Predictive maintenance without an owned, automated response is a dashboard nobody acts on until the line stops anyway. It's the same failure mode Gartner points to across agentic AI projects broadly: the model works, the decision loop around it doesn't.

The plants closing that gap aren't buying a better model. They're assigning a name to the alert.

When your last predictive-maintenance alert fired, how many hours passed before anyone with authority touched it?
